planting.note: Root semi-hardwood tip cuttings or set out container plants in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; because 'Aurea' does not twine, install a trellis, wire, or fence support at planting time and begin tying in the young canes right away.

directions: 'Aurea' is a clear golden-yellow-flowered selection of the South African Cape honeysuckle, grown identically to the orange-red species but valued for a brighter, more unusual color break in a scrambling shrub-vine. Like the type, it does not climb by tendrils or twining and must be tied to a support or left to sprawl as an informal mounding hedge or bank cover. Flowering is concentrated from fall into spring, a season when few other tropical vines are in bloom, and the tubular flowers draw hummingbirds reliably through the cooler months. Established plants shrug off heat, drought, salt spray, and poor alkaline soils, and typically resprout from the base after a hard zone 9 freeze cuts the top growth back.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

planting.note: Set rooted cuttings or container plants in spring into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; 'Apricot' stays noticeably more compact and self-contained than the straight species, so it can be grown as an unsupported informal shrub or trained onto a smaller trellis than the rangy species form requires.

directions: 'Apricot' bears soft peachy-apricot tubular flowers, a gentler pastel departure from the vivid orange-red of typical Cape honeysuckle, and a more restrained, self-branching habit that holds up well as a freestanding shrub without heavy tying. Native South African stock behind this selection blooms in flushes from fall through spring, coinciding with the period when migrating and overwintering hummingbirds most need nectar along the Gulf Coast. It thrives in poor, sandy, or alkaline soil and full sun, and rank, over-fertilized growth actually reduces bloom, so lean conditions are preferred. In zone 9 winters it can freeze to the ground but regenerates quickly from the roots with the return of warm weather.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

planting.note: Root semi-hardwood cuttings or plant container stock in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; because 'Coccinea' scrambles rather than climbs, tie the developing canes to a fence or trellis as they extend, or allow the plant to mound informally as a sprawling hedge.

directions: 'Coccinea' is a deep orange-red, almost tomato-toned selection of Cape honeysuckle, more saturated and intense than the standard orange-red species form, from a South African evergreen scrambling shrub of the Bignoniaceae. It carries the same tubular, hummingbird-favored flowers in dense terminal clusters, flowering heaviest from autumn through spring. As with the species, it does not twine or grip a support on its own and needs to be tied in or grown as an unsupported sprawling mass on a slope or bank. It tolerates heat, salt spray, drought, and poor alkaline soils with ease, and recovers from root level after hard freezes in zone 9.
sources: South African National Biodiversity Institute (SANBI) - PlantZAfrica

planting.note: Root stem cuttings or plant container specimens in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun against a strong trellis, pergola, or fence; give the plant two full growing seasons to establish a woody framework before expecting a heavy flowering display.

directions: Zimbabwe creeper is a vigorous, sprawling scrambling shrub-vine collected historically from the ruins of Great Zimbabwe and the coastal thickets near Sofala, Mozambique, closely related to the more familiar pink trumpet vine (Podranea ricasoliana) but distinguished by its paler, more lavender-pink, yellow-throated flowers with fine darker veining. It typically flowers in two distinct flushes, one in early summer and a second in fall, followed by long slender seed pods, and the blooms carry a light fragrance that the more common Podranea ricasoliana generally lacks. Because it scrambles rather than climbs by tendrils, tie the long canes to a sturdy support as they extend, or let the plant sprawl over a bank or low wall. It performs best in Gulf Coast zone 9-11 gardens in full sun with regular moisture during establishment, tapering to only occasional supplemental water once mature.
sources: South African National Biodiversity Institute (SANBI) - PlantZAfrica

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container-grown vines in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade next to a sturdy arbor, wall, or pergola; the vine climbs by branched tendrils tipped with adhesive disks and will attach directly to masonry, wood, or wire without additional training.

directions: 'Rivers' is a garden hybrid between Distictis buccinatoria and Distictis laxiflora, combining the vigor and bloom size of the blood-red trumpet vine parent with the color-shifting, fragrant flowers of the vanilla trumpet vine parent. Its large, flared trumpet flowers open a rich purple-mauve with a bright yellow throat and gradually fade to pink as they age, so a single mature plant typically displays several flower colors at once across its canopy. It blooms in flushes nearly continuously through the warm months rather than concentrating into one or two distinct seasonal peaks, making it one of the more reliably colorful evergreen vines for covering large structures in zone 9-11 gardens. Because it is a vigorous, glossy-leaved climber capable of scaling 20 feet or more, it needs a substantial support and benefits from an annual thinning after the main growth flush to keep it from overwhelming smaller structures.

planting.note: Set container-grown vines in spring in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to partial shade beside a fence, arbor, or trellis; the vine climbs by tendrils and clasps supports on its own once established, needing only occasional tying while young.

directions: Vanilla trumpet vine is native to seasonally dry, mid-elevation woodlands of southern Mexico (Chiapas, Oaxaca, Puebla, Veracruz) and northern Nicaragua, and is distinguished from its relative Distictis buccinatoria by tubular-bell flowers that carry a distinct, pleasant vanilla fragrance. The blooms open a dark lavender-purple and fade gradually through pale lilac to nearly cream-white as they age, so clusters in different stages of aging give the vine a soft, multi-toned appearance through the warm months. It is somewhat more shade-tolerant and less rampant than Distictis buccinatoria, making it a good choice for a lightly shaded arbor or fence where a slightly less overwhelming bignonia-family vine is wanted. Established plants tolerate brief dips into the mid-20s Fahrenheit, typically defoliating but resprouting from older wood, which suits zone 9 Gulf Coast winters.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center
